rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds and elute strongly retained compounds, with time for a final high-organic hold. The retention and resolution pattern will guide targeted gradient and temperature adjustments.
Halve the gradient duration to shorten the run while testing how much of the substantial resolution margin remains. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the gradient-slope effect.

A modestly shallower gradient should improve the critical separation while keeping the last peak below the apparent 10-minute time-penalty threshold. This tests the resolution–time boundary with temperature and endpoints unchanged.

Increase temperature by 5 °C to test whether selectivity improves the remaining critical pair while preserving the penalty-free elution time. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect.

The critical pair converged sharply at 45 °C; testing 55 °C may separate it again after an elution-order reversal. The other gaps appear to offer enough margin for this selectivity shift, while the run should remain free of a time penalty.

After the apparent elution-order reversal, a steeper gradient may now widen the critical pair rather than compress it. Shortening to 12 minutes tests this direction while retaining the favorable temperature and avoiding a time penalty.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to improve the pair currently at R = 1.59 while aiming to keep the R = 1.52 pair above 1.5. This tests a nearby alternative to the maximum-scoring method with ample time-penalty margin.

The maximum CRF is already reached, so test whether a higher starting organic fraction offers another fully resolved method. The longer gradient should help preserve separation while the higher starting strength limits retention time.

Extend the successful higher-starting-organic trend while lengthening the gradient to preserve separation. This tests for a larger minimum-resolution margin at the already maximal CRF, with last-peak elution expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Lengthen the gradient slightly to improve the newly limiting pair at R = 1.41. The other critical pair has some margin at R = 1.74, and the last peak is expected to remain below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a shallower gradient adjacent to injection 8 to improve its R = 1.77 pair while checking that the R = 1.57 pair remains adequately resolved. This may provide another maximum-scoring method with less early-peak compression than injection 10.

Test whether 60 °C widens the temperature-sensitive critical pair, using a shallower gradient and low starting organic fraction to protect the other close pair. The maximum CRF is already established; this explores an alternative with potentially greater separation margin.

Explore the lower-temperature selectivity branch relative to injection 3, where warming worsened the limiting separation. This tests whether cooling can yield another fully resolved method while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a shallower gradient at 40 °C to improve the limiting separation from injection 3, while raising the starting organic fraction to offset the increased retention. This explores another potentially maximum-scoring method without relying on the narrow selectivity window near 55 °C.

Use a shallower gradient to improve the R = 1.42 critical pair from injection 14, with a higher starting organic fraction to offset the retention increase. This tests whether full resolution and penalty-free elution can also be achieved at 40 °C.

Extend the successful 40 °C trend with a higher starting organic fraction and shallower gradient to seek more resolution margin. Monitor the increasingly compressed early peaks while targeting last-peak elution below 10 minutes.

Test a gradient slope between injections 9 and 10, aiming to raise the limiting resolution above 1.5 while eluting sooner than injection 10. This seeks another maximum-scoring method with a useful balance of separation and time margins.

This preserves injection 6’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope, with the gradient still continuing beyond its last observed peak. It should retain the maximum CRF while testing a lower final organic fraction and shorter programmed gradient.

Preserve the proven gradient slope while lowering the endpoint further; the gradient should still extend beyond the last peak at the outlet. This tests another maximum-scoring method with a lower final organic fraction.

Keep the proven slope but begin the final hold after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether a 50% organic endpoint still elutes the last compound below 10 minutes while preserving the maximum CRF.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to improve its earlier critical pair while retaining adequate separation of the later pair. Last-peak elution should remain below 10 minutes, potentially preserving maximum CRF with balanced resolution margins.
Slightly steepen injection 8’s gradient to shorten retention and potentially balance its two closest separations. This tests another maximum-CRF candidate with a last-peak time near 8 minutes.

Slightly steepen injection 22’s gradient to shorten the run and bring its two closest resolutions toward a balanced margin above 1.5. The gradient should continue beyond the last peak, avoiding an endpoint-hold effect.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests whether an earlier final hold can shorten last-peak retention relative to a long, shallow gradient while maintaining full resolution. The critical pairs should elute during the gradient, but their response to the shallower slope remains to be measured.

Match injection 22’s successful gradient slope with a lower endpoint, keeping the outlet gradient active beyond its last peak at 8.00 minutes. This should preserve full resolution and the maximum CRF of 1.000.
